label: Synchronization: barrier, critical, atomic, single vs masked (no barrier)
objective: Given a parallel region, choose the construct each need calls for: order all threads (barrier), make a code section mutually exclusive (critical), make one memory update indivisible (atomic), run a block once (single, with a barrier) or on the primary thread (masked, without one); and predict hangs and races from the barrier rules.
why_needed: n8 (reductions) is explained as 'private copy + combine', n10 (overhead) needs the cost model of barriers and critical sections, n11 (tasks) reuses barrier/taskwait, n12 (memory model) builds on which constructs synchronize.

prerequisites.why: race definition: what the constructs remove
one team, constructs divide or order its work

motivation: Every thread has computed a partial result. Now they must combine them into one shared total, and then thread 0 must print it. Each step is a different kind of ordering problem: 'one at a time' (mutual exclusion), 'indivisible' (atomic) and 'everyone is done' (barrier). Getting them mixed up gives either a race or a hang.
outline: Recall from n2: a race is two unordered accesses to one location, one a write. Synchronization constructs create the missing ordering.

barrier: all threads of the team wait until all have arrived. Rule (definition): a barrier must be met by all threads or none, and every thread must meet the same sequence of worksharing regions and barriers. Implicit barriers (guarantee): end of parallel, for, sections, single (unless nowait). No barrier: masked, critical, atomic, task.

critical: mutual exclusion on a code section; all unnamed criticals share one name, so unrelated unnamed sections exclude each other; named ones are independent. Nesting a critical inside a same-name critical is not allowed.

atomic: one indivisible memory update on one location (read / write / update x op= expr / capture). Default memory order relaxed (5.0+); it always does a strong flush of that location. Covers one location: two coupled updates need critical.

single vs masked: single is one thread, not necessarily the primary, with an implicit barrier at its end; masked (master is deprecated) is the primary thread and has no barrier, so data it produces needs an explicit barrier before others may read it.
Cost model (simplification): atomic maps to a hardware read-modify-write, critical to a lock; both are correct; contention decides which is cheaper. Not a spec guarantee.
Connection forward: a reduction (n8) is 'each thread its own copy, one combine', which avoids both critical and atomic in the loop body.

claims.text: A barrier region must be encountered by all threads of the team or by none, and the sequence of worksharing and barrier regions must be the same for every thread.
An implicit barrier ends parallel, for, sections and single regions unless nowait is given; masked, critical, atomic and task imply no barrier.
claims.boundary: nowait removes it; single with nowait therefore needs an explicit barrier if others depend on its result.

claims.text: critical regions with the same name are executed as if by one thread at a time; unnamed critical constructs behave as if they all had one identical name.
claims.boundary: Named regions with different names may run concurrently; nesting a critical in a same-name critical is not permitted and the spec says that restriction is not sufficient to prevent deadlock.

claims.text: atomic makes a single storage update indivisible; update forms are x++, x--, ++x, --x, x binop= expr, x = x binop expr, x = expr binop x (plus read, write and capture forms).
claims.boundary: expr must not access x; only x's update is atomic, not the evaluation of expr or any other location.

claims.text: Without a memory-order clause an atomic construct is relaxed (OpenMP 5.0+) but still performs a strong flush of the location of x on entry and exit.
claims.boundary: OpenMP 4.5 had no memory-order clauses; relaxed does not order other locations (n12).

claims.text: single is executed by exactly one thread of the team, not necessarily the primary; masked (master is deprecated since 5.1) is executed by the primary thread and implies no barrier.
claims.boundary: gcc 13 accepts masked in C although _OPENMP reports 201511.

claims.text: atomic is usually cheaper than critical because it maps to a hardware read-modify-write instruction rather than a lock.
claims.boundary: not a spec guarantee; under heavy contention both serialize, and false sharing can dominate either.

misconceptions.repair: It protects a code section by name: two unrelated unnamed critical sections exclude each other, and two named ones around the same variable do not. Name them by the data they guard.

misconceptions.text: atomic protects the whole statement, including a second update or a function call.
misconceptions.repair: It makes exactly one storage update indivisible. Show total += f(x): only the += on total is atomic; f runs unprotected. Two coupled updates need critical.

misconceptions.text: masked/master ends with a barrier like single.
misconceptions.repair: It does not. Show masked writing a shared variable and other threads reading it: a race unless an explicit barrier follows.

misconceptions.text: A barrier inside an if that only some threads take is fine because the others just skip it.
misconceptions.repair: All-or-none rule: the threads that arrive wait forever for the ones that never come. Demonstrate the hang mentally with 2 threads.
single is whichever thread gets there first (unspecified); masked is the primary thread.

variants.question:
Answer (a), (b) and (c) for this region (total is shared, mine is private).
(a) Is there a data race on total? Explain why or why not, and whether the printf is guaranteed to see all four contributions.
(b) Which lighter construct could replace critical here, and why is it enough?
(c) Now the body becomes { total += mine; log[count++] = mine; } with log and count shared. Is your construct from (b) still enough? Explain.
variants.answer: (a) No data race on total: critical makes the update mutually exclusive, so the accesses are ordered and never overlap; the printf runs after the region-end barrier. (b) #pragma omp atomic on total += mine: one indivisible memory update, and it suffices because that is the only shared update. (c) If the body becomes { total += mine; log[count++] = mine; }, atomic no longer suffices: count++ and the write to log[count] are two coupled operations on two locations, and atomic covers a single update. Mutual exclusion around both (critical) is needed.
required: critical (or atomic) orders the updates so they never overlap: no race; printf is after the region-end barrier
atomic suffices for the single update total += mine
atomic covers exactly one memory update; the coupled count++ and log write need critical
accepted: describes atomic as a hardware read-modify-write
proposes a reduction for (b) as an alternative
disqualifying: claims atomic can cover both updates in (c)
says the race remains under critical because threads run in nondeterministic order

variants.question:
Answer (a), (b) and (c) for this histogram (hist is shared).
(a) Is there a data race on hist? Explain why or why not.
(b) Which lighter construct could replace critical here, and why is it enough?
(c) Now the body becomes { hist[b]++; if (hist[b] == 1) nonempty++; } with nonempty shared. Is your construct from (b) still enough? Explain.
variants.answer: (a) There is no race: critical serializes every increment, whatever bin. (b) #pragma omp atomic on hist[b]++ suffices: each increment is one indivisible update of one location, and different bins can proceed concurrently. (c) If the body becomes { hist[b]++; if (hist[b] == 1) nonempty++; } atomic no longer suffices: the increment, the read-back and the second counter are coupled operations on two locations, so critical around all of them is needed.
required: critical serializes the increments so no race
atomic on hist[b]++ suffices: one indivisible update of one location
the coupled read-back and second counter need critical

hints: A race needs two unordered accesses, one a write. What does critical do to the order of the accesses to total?
atomic makes exactly one memory update indivisible (x op= expr). Count the locations updated in (c).

Worked: in (c) thread A reads count, thread B reads the same count, both write log[count] and both bump count: lost update. atomic could cover count++ alone, but log[...] uses the value read before the increment: only mutual exclusion around both operations is correct.

variants.question: Which of the marked constructs are followed by an implicit barrier?
variants.code:
#pragma omp parallel
{
    #pragma omp single
    setup();                 /* (1) */
    #pragma omp masked
    log_start();             /* (2) */
    #pragma omp for
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        a[i] = f(i);         /* (3) */
    use(a);                  /* every thread reads all of a */
}

hints: Which construct is documented as having no implied barrier on entry or exit?

variants.question: A team fills a shared array buf with a work-sharing loop. Then thread 0 alone must print a summary of buf before any thread starts the next work-sharing loop, which overwrites buf. Write the constructs between the two loops and justify each: where is a barrier needed, and where is one already there?
variants.answer: The first omp for ends with an implicit barrier, so buf is complete when any thread leaves it. Then #pragma omp masked (or single) around the print. masked has no barrier, so an explicit #pragma omp barrier must follow before the second loop, otherwise other threads may start overwriting buf while thread 0 is still printing. With single instead, its implicit barrier does that job (but single is not necessarily thread 0).
required: the first loop's implicit barrier makes buf complete before the print
masked has no barrier: an explicit barrier (or single's implicit barrier) is needed before the overwrite
disqualifying: places no barrier between the print and the second loop

hints: Which of the two loops' boundaries already has a barrier?
What does masked promise about the other threads while thread 0 prints?
Worked: threads 1-3 leave the masked block immediately and enter loop 2; without a barrier they overwrite buf[i] while thread 0 reads it.

variants.question: histogram-sync: make the parallel histogram race-free with the cheapest sufficient construct, keep the serial result exactly, and explain in one paragraph why the tests passing does not by itself prove the absence of a race.
variants.answer: atomic update on hist[b]++ (or a critical section, correct but slower under contention; or a per-thread private histogram combined at the end, which previews n8). The explanation must name the two unordered accesses that the construct orders.
required: uses atomic (or critical/reduction) on the shared increment
explains which accesses were unordered and how the construct orders them
states that passing runs are evidence, not proof

hints: Which single statement updates shared memory?

Worked: #pragma omp atomic directly above hist[b]++; different bins proceed concurrently.
